AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult.
  • Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis.
  • Industry observers note that the new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.

Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.

Industry observers note that the new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.

AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records.

Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.

In a recent development, confirming bladder cancer presently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.

To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.

Sources indicate that the researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.

AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases.

The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.

The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.

Industry observers note that the AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.

For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.

According to recent reports, these findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.

It has been revealed that another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.

Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.

A Newly introduced Approach to Early Cancer Screening.

Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).

This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.

Sources indicate that for example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.

PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022.".

"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods.".

Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?

Industry observers note that the potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.

According to recent reports, dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.

"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.

"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved.".

Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.

"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages.".

More Research Needed Before Clinical Use.

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.

All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.

Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.

"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.

Recent findings suggest that "But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions.".

The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.

The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.

The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Upgrade 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller patch. When Battlefield Studios revealed it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

It has been revealed that the end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

It has been revealed that the other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

It has been revealed that and, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Recent findings suggest that finally, the revision makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Read on below for the 1.1.3.5 change log.

#155167. AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1343 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed.
  • For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works.
  • But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," claims York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity.".

A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI.

Industry observers note that the York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

Recent findings suggest that if these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Recent findings suggest that their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story.

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

Industry observers note that "The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," claims Kar.

The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

In a recent development, kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly vital as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

It has been revealed that "The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior.

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," states Muzellec.

Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

It has been revealed that the concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.

Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain.

Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.

By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," states Kar. "This is especially key for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline.".

It has been revealed that A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is key for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a fresh approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.

The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know what’s nice about Grand Theft Auto 6 having such a monumental, far-reaching release? No, it’s not the literal billions of dollars it’s bringing in, though I’m sure nobody at Rockstar or Take-Two minds that. The best thing about having so many eyes on your game at once is that, if any bugs were missed during the game’s QA testing phases, they will eventually be caught with an almost mathematical certainty.

Considering the sheer scope and density of GTA 6’s world, it shouldn’t be especially surprising that there’s a decent amount of bugs, errors, and assorted unintentional annoyances floating around, some of which are more severe than others, causing problems with the game’s progression and critical systems or even hard crashes. Thankfully, Rockstar devs are still in the trenches even after release, hunting down bugs as they rear their ugly heads. Feel free to make your own Starship Troopers reference.

In an announcement posted to the official Rockstar Support blog today, the dev revealed the latest launch updates and fixes applied to GTA 6 as of this morning that squash several severe bugs. This update applies to both the PlayStation 5 and XBOX Series X/S versions of the game, and should either already be applied or ready to be applied next time you boot up.

According to the Rockstar Support blog, this new update covers seven critical bullet points’ worth of updates. First and foremost, an unspecified number of concerns that, when triggered, caused the game to crash, have been dealt with, so it should be more stable going forward.

Sources indicate that next, a bug that caused in-game weather to stay static for noticeably long stretches has been fixed, so you should be back to seeing regular, consistent weather patterns throughout Vice City. On a more notable note, another bug that prevented the game from autosaving properly has been patched, so progression loss should be less of a concern.

The most notable fix in the patch squashes a bug that was preventing mission-critical phone calls from triggering. Players afflicted with this bug weren’t having phone calls that progressed the story or unlocked mission content come in, which was a major progression bug. On a similarly critical level, a bug that prevented players from properly losing their current Wanted level has been dealt with as well.

The most vital fix in the patch squashes a bug that was preventing mission-critical phone calls from triggering.

Finally, in a couple of relatively smaller fixes, a bug that prevented players from using the deadlift bar in the gym, alongside a bug that prevented partners from handing over fence-able bags, have both been dealt with, so you can get your gains and sell your illicit substances.

It’s good to see Rockstar on the case, dealing with these severe bugs, but as I said, GTA 6’s world is gargantuan, and there’s probably going to be a lot more bug reports flowing in for the foreseeable future, especially if and when the game receives any substantial additional content.

Industry observers note that in addition to the bugs that have already been squashed, numerous reports have been coming in around the web of other annoyances, confusions, and assorted weirdness. For example, some players have reported NPCs walking into walls, while others report small, incidental objects floating in the air.

It has been revealed that there’s also been some reports of graphical hiccups, mostly related to unpleasant pop-in. Clothing and cosmetic items may occasionally pop-in during gameplay, large vehicles like ships and planes may pop-in at a distance, and character models may appear distorted or low-poly for a split-second when loading in cutscenes. Most of this stuff is incidental at best, with some like the unintentional first-person view bug actually being popular, but hopefully, if anything more severe crops up, Rockstar will hop on promptly.

The 2026 Esports Awards honoured two British figures from the streaming and broadcast side of the scene. Caedrel is a League of Legends streamer and co-streamer. Gaskin works as a caster.

The ceremony took place on the evening of 17 November at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts of Miami-Dade County. It is the scene’s main end-of-season awards show. The event began in London in 2016.

At Worlds 2026, Caedrel was the top co-streamer for both hours watched and peak viewers, according to Esports Charts.

According to recent reports, his co-stream success came in a softer year for the tournament overall. Worlds 2026 peaked at 3.98 million viewers, which was 41% lower than the previous year. Caedrel’s numbers show how much attention a single co-streamer can hold even when the event’s headline peak falls.

In a recent development, gaskin was not the only caster honoured in Miami. The other broadcast honours went to Alex ‘Machine’ Richardson for Play-by-Play Caster of the Year, Iain Chambers for Host of the Year and Anthony ‘NAMELESS’ Wheeler for Analyst of the Year. iShowSpeed was named Streamer of the Year.

Counter-Strike featured prominently among the industry prizes. Vitality’s award as best organisation came alongside Esports PC Player of the Year for Mathieu ‘ZywOo’ Herbaut. OpTic Texas were named Esports Team of the Year.

BLAST, which stages many of its events in Europe, was named Esports Tournament Organiser of the Year.

It has been revealed that vitality’s results through the year back up their award. They beat Spirit to win IEM Rio 2026 on 19 April, giving them back-to-back ESL Grand Slam titles. ZywOo took his 31st career HLTV MVP award at that event.

"When I won this award in 2023, I never thanked my parents" 😅❤️.

Sources indicate that the team’s form held into the autumn. Vitality swept MOUZ 3-0 in the ESL Pro League Season 24 grand final on 11 October. That was their second title in a row after winning StarSeries Fall in September.

In a recent development, the PGL Major Singapore 2026 runs from 25 November to 13 December with 32 teams and a US$1,250,000 prize pool, The Kallang reported. The final stages will be played at the Singapore Indoor Stadium from 10 to 13 December.

Industry observers note that escape the Baby Alarm has its own charm, from the moment you see the graphics that come with it. This narrative-driven puzzler is all about becoming a parent, losing yourself, being exhausted, and trying to find your own way to heal. The gameplay is a mix of almost comic book-like stories to scroll through and puzzles that make sense if you look around for a bit.

Many of these moments are very relatable if you have ever had a baby. Organising your baby's items, trying to make a mobile, cleaning your house. There are lots of moments that show the frame of mind of a newborn. Some honest panels of struggling to believe in yourself. Moments of needing to clean your house so that you can then watch over your baby. There's even a sort of boss fight full of puzzles where you are trying to defeat your own self-doubt.

It's a very interesting game, full of colour, and the various puzzles are really well thought out. Each of the puzzles does have three hints as well as a screenshot that shows you the answer, if you do get stuck. There aren't often timers, but there is sometimes someone who will knock out the things that you've done, so you need to put them back in. The puzzles have a nice variety and flow to them.

I found the little storybook elements of the game to be lovely too; some of them feel very empowering. There is a lot of content in Escape the Baby Alarm - from the puzzles to the chapters to little diary entries that are written by the developer, really showing personal moments and their own feelings when it comes to the birth of their baby. This very much feels like fumbling through someone's diary!

It has been revealed that escape the Baby Alarm is all about discovering who you are after having a baby, finding your own voice, and making sure that you are reflecting on your own self as well, so that you can be the best version of yourself. It's trippy, in the best sort of way, and really draws you in.

Download now! Escape the Baby Alarm.

#155161. Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1585 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to upcoming research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.
  • Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to upcoming research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.

Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20. These early changes could remain largely unnoticed for decades before eventually contributing to the disease.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear. They also raise the possibility of preventing the cancer by slowing the growth of abnormal blood cells long before the disease takes hold.

Blood Samples Reveal Leukemia's Hidden History.

According to recent reports, published in Nature, the study was conducted by researchers at the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL). By examining blood samples collected over many years, including some obtained as long as 15 years before diagnosis, the team pieced together a detailed history of how leukemia develops.

According to recent reports, the scientists treated these stored samples as a kind of genetic fossil record. Using highly sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical models, they worked backward to estimate when cancer-related mutations first appeared, how quickly the affected cells multiplied, and how they competed with other blood cells as the disease approached.

AML is an aggressive blood cancer that affects approximately 2,700 people in the UK annually. Its outlook is often poor, with only about one in six patients surviving at least five years after diagnosis.

In a recent development, scientists have long known that many otherwise healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations associated with leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, does not necessarily lead to cancer. In fact, most people with these mutations never develop AML. Until now, researchers have struggled to understand why some individuals progress to leukemia while others do not, partly because they lacked a detailed record of the genetic changes occurring in the years before diagnosis.

According to recent reports, to investigate, the team turned to samples from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS). That project involved approximately 50,000 women who provided blood samples annually for as long as 11 years.

For the new analysis, researchers examined samples from 47 women who eventually developed AML, with an average age at diagnosis of 72. They compared these findings with samples from 46 similar women who remained free of blood cancer.

Cancer Mutations Can Remain Hidden for Decades.

According to recent reports, the results revealed an extraordinary timeline. In two-thirds of the women who developed AML, the earliest mutation contributing to the disease was estimated to have occurred before their 20th birthday.

At first, the altered blood cells multiplied extremely slowly, sometimes taking several years just to double in number. But as additional cancer-driving mutations accumulated, their growth accelerated dramatically.

Each upcoming mutation typically increased the rate of growth by roughly two to three times. By the time cells had acquired four mutations capable of driving cancer, their populations could double within weeks instead of years.

Perhaps even more surprising was how consistently these populations behaved.

Researchers found that groups of genetically related blood cells, known as clones, generally expanded at predictable rates once they became established. Their growth tended to slow only when they faced limited space or competition from another clone that was multiplying more quickly.

It has been revealed that this consistency could have notable medical implications. By measuring the growth of a particular clone using just a few blood samples, scientists may be able to estimate how large that population will become many years into the future, potentially even decades later.

A Hidden Warning Sign of Leukemia.

The researchers also identified a striking pattern that appeared in some patients well before leukemia was diagnosed.

Industry observers note that in at least one-third of AML cases, a single population of mutated blood cells had grown so extensively that it dominated the blood years before diagnosis. Scientists call this process a "somatic sweep.".

None of the women in the comparison group who remained free of blood cancer indicated the same pattern.

The researchers then examined data from the UK Biobank and confirmed that people showing evidence of these sweeps faced a substantially greater risk of developing AML.

This finding suggests that somatic sweeps could serve as an important early warning sign. However, conventional genetic testing can miss them because the mutations involved are sometimes incorrectly classified as inherited genetic variations.

Professor Jamie Blundell, who led the research at the University of Cambridge's Early Cancer Institute, explained how the team reconstructed the disease's history.

"Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood's evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now.".

In a recent development, he added: "Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia.".

Could Leukemia Be Prevented Before It Develops?

The discovery could change how doctors approach a disease that often appears to develop with little warning.

In a recent development, dr. Caroline Watson, the study's first author and a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute, emphasized the contrast between the sudden impact of a leukemia diagnosis and the decades of biological changes that may precede it.

"As a hematologist, I've seen how suddenly AML can change someone's life. This study shows that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways.".

Watson is also an Honorary Consultant Haematologist who treats patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic at Addenbrooke's Hospital. The clinic is the first in Europe dedicated to leukemia prevention and already monitors people whose blood cell mutations place them at increased risk of developing the disease.

She added: "At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today's findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible.".

Years of Blood Samples Unlock Fresh Cancer Clues.

A major reason the researchers could reconstruct leukemia's development was the availability of blood samples collected repeatedly from the same individuals over many years.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led the original UKCTOCS project, highlighted the unexpected scientific value of those samples.

Recent findings suggest that "While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement.".

Sources indicate that the women who developed AML received their diagnoses between ages 53 and 83. Because the researchers did not have blood samples taken at the time of diagnosis, they could not directly examine the final stage of the disease's development in those patients.

According to recent reports, the findings also showed that not every case followed the same extended timeline of detectable changes. In approximately one in five cases, growing populations of mutated blood cells became detectable only one to two years before diagnosis. This suggests that some patients may have a much shorter opportunity for early intervention.

A New Path Toward Preventing Leukemia.

Despite these limitations, the results offer an encouraging possibility: leukemia risk might be reduced by intervening long before the disease develops.

According to the researchers' mathematical models, even a modest reduction in the growth of high-risk blood cell clones could have a substantial effect over time. Because these cells multiply exponentially, slowing their expansion across the ten or more years between a second cancer-driving mutation and diagnosis could significantly reduce the likelihood that they eventually progress to leukemia.

This raises the prospect of preventive treatments designed to restrain dangerous cell populations rather than waiting until they have developed into cancer.

According to recent reports, the next challenge is determining whether such an approach can be used safely and effectively in people identified as having an elevated risk of AML. Although the research provides a promising framework for earlier detection and prevention, clinical studies will be needed to establish whether slowing these abnormal cells actually prevents leukemia in humans.

The research was primarily supported by UK Research & Innovation and Cancer Research UK.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the hacker behind GTA 6's massive 2022 leak was sentenced to seven years in prison on November 23.
  • Recent findings suggest that as Dexerto reports, the 21-year-old was released on licence after the court took account of the time he'd already spent in custody.
  • It has been revealed that kurtaj was part of the Lapsus$ hacking group and had been detained for years while his case worked its way through the courts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the hacker behind GTA 6's massive 2022 leak was sentenced to seven years in prison on November 23. But instead of returning to prison, Arion Kurtaj walked out of Woolwich Crown Court that day, just four days after Rockstar's long-awaited game launched.

Recent findings suggest that as Dexerto reports, the 21-year-old was released on licence after the court took account of the time he'd already spent in custody. He's also subject to a five-year order limiting what he can do online. So while the sentence sounds surprising, his release doesn't mean the charges were dropped.

It has been revealed that kurtaj was part of the Lapsus$ hacking group and had been detained for years while his case worked its way through the courts. In December 2023, he was placed in a secure hospital after being deemed unfit to stand trial. A later assessment found him fit to plead, and he was moved to prison in January 2026.

On November 16, he pleaded guilty to a series of offences connected to cyberattacks on Rockstar Games and other companies. DualShockers covered his guilty plea at the time, noting how close it was to GTA 6's November 19 release. His sentencing followed exactly one week later.

Recent findings suggest that kurtaj had already spent enough time in custody to be released on licence rather than sent back to prison. Walking out of court doesn't mean he can go straight back to his old online life.

Sources indicate that he's now subject to a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order restricting his online activity, including a ban on using Discord and Telegram. It's a significant condition for someone who committed cyberattacks while already on bail.

Walking out of court doesn't mean he can go straight back to his old online life.

Justice Turner also warned Kurtaj about wasting his abilities on further offences. The judge described him as talented and urged him not to spend his life repeatedly returning to prison.

The case also involved attacks on Uber, Revolut, and BT/EE. According to the UK Crown Prosecution Service, Kurtaj's activities exposed sensitive information and disrupted business systems. In the BT/EE case, prosecutors linked his intrusion to unauthorized SIM swaps, which could let criminals take over other people's calls and messages. He also admitted to possessing a mobile phone in prison, an offence dating to March 2026.

Back in September 2022, Kurtaj obtained 90 GTA 6 gameplay videos from Rockstar's systems and posted the footage online under the name TeaPotUberHacker. It gave everyone an early, unfinished look at the next Grand Theft Auto, long before Rockstar was ready to show it off. Rockstar sources reportedly confirmed the footage was genuine shortly afterwards.

In a recent development, one of the stranger details is how he did it. Kurtaj was already on bail for other cybercrimes and had been moved to a hotel for his own protection. From there, he used a phone, the hotel's television Wi-Fi, and an Amazon Fire Stick to carry out further attacks, including the one on Rockstar.

It has been revealed that the leaked footage indicated parts of Vice City and early gameplay involving the game's two leads. Kurtaj also tried to blackmail Rockstar by threatening to release the game's source code unless the company contacted him. The 90 videos were released; the source code was what he threatened to put out next.

The damage wasn't just about fans seeing the game early. Rockstar reportedly spent around $5 million and thousands of staff hours dealing with the breach, according to Dexerto. That was on top of the disruption to other companies targeted in the same hacking spree.

Recent findings suggest that those clips spread across the internet more than four years before GTA 6's November 19 release. Now that the game is finally out, Kurtaj's case has reached sentencing too. He's left prison, but the online restrictions attached to his release will continue for another five years.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

According to recent reports, another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off latest gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

In a recent development, battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Recent findings suggest that ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

In a recent development, there’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is at the moment in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

Industry observers note that for context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its problems elsewhere, and BF Studios indicates it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

According to recent reports, redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (373 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.
  • Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis.
  • A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently new cases occur.

Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's.

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

Unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

Industry observers note that "While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often fresh cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi noted.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes.".

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar spent a long time working on Grand Theft Auto 6, and it indicates through the games many small details. There are tons of hidden easter eggs and secrets scattered across Leonida, and some of them connect to previous GTA titles.

Recent findings suggest that more specifically, there are a decent number that connect back to GTA 5. Have you ever wondered what happened to Michael’s boat? Who took the blame for the murder of Floyd and Debora?

Industry observers note that thanks to GTA 6, we now the answers to these questions, and there are many more connections to GTA 5 that you might not have discovered. Everything is connected after all.

If you played GTA 5, odds are you spent a great deal of time exploring the map and going from town to town. It was quite a significant map, but you wouldn’t have spent your entire time in the city, so you probably recognize Grapeseed and the Grand Senora Desert.

Industry observers note that grapeseed is a small town in the northern part of the GTA 5 map, with it residing in Blaine County. The Grand Senora Desert is a much larger area, but it also resides in Blaine County.

Industry observers note that while exploring the many buildings that you can enter in GTA 6, you can wander into a few trailers, and some of them have postcards that link Leonida to Los Santos. You can find postcards specifically for Grapeseed and Grand Senora Desert.

According to recent reports, you get a lot of phone calls in GTA 5. Many missions start with you getting a call, and then proceeding to head to some location. Because of this, if you have played the story, you will have heard Michael’s ringtone quite a bit.

Industry observers note that well, if you feel so inclined, and want to stay true to the spirit of GTA 5, you can have Michael’s ringtone in GTA 6. All you need to do is go into your phone’s settings, choose the ringtone option, and then select the one called Wind Chimes.

This ringtone is exactly the same as Michael’s from GTA 5, giving you that classic GTA feeling from 13 years ago when you played the campaign for GTA 5.

It has been revealed that one of the best easter eggs in GTA 6 is that you can find Michael’s boat from GTA 5, and you don’t really need to go all that far. In fact, you have to stick rather close to home, because it is sitting right outside Jason’s house at the start of the game.

Michael ends up having his boat stolen in GTA 5, and you never learn what happens to it. Well, it somehow found its way to Leonida and ended up in Jason’s yard.

If you decide to climb up on the boat, you can see that a screen is still active on it. This screen demonstrates the shores of Los Santos from GTA 5, seemingly proving that this is indeed the same boat that was stolen from Michael all those years ago.

According to recent reports, do you remember Fabien? He teaches Michael how to do yoga in GTA 5, and is known for having some rather… suggestive yoga poses. Throughout GTA 5, you can perform yoga as Michael either at his house or at the peak of Mount Gordo.

Recent findings suggest that fabien has been doing well since the events of GTA 5, and you can see what he has been up to thanks to his article in one of the game’s magazines. This is also an easter egg that you can find outside of Jason’s house.

It has been revealed that go out onto the porch, and open the magazine that is on the table near the workout equipment. Flip through the pages, and you will find that Fabien has been doing well. He has been on an “epic pilgrimage of enlightenment.”.

It is a little ambiguous as to if the Mount Chiliad Mystery in GTA 5 was ever solved. While there is a means of seeing a UFO from it, it didn’t have a narrative conclusion, so it is debated on whether or not it was ever completed.

In a recent development, however, this mystery is mentioned in GTA 6, and it is on a vehicle. You can find an RV in Leonida that is covered in phrases like, “Don’t be fooled,” and “There’s no driving away.”.

What connects this to Mount Chiliad is the eye symbol. It is the same eye symbol that is found at the top of the Mount Chiliad mural, making it seem like the mystery was never fully solved, or maybe that is just what Rockstar wants us to think.

There are some small nods to GTA 5 hidden throughout GTA 6, and one that is easy to overlook is a small book review for a novel sitting in Jason’s house. The book in question is titled Lethal By Design: A Liberty City Memoir, written by Tom Everett.

This book connects to the events of GTA 4 and Niko Bellic - a fan-favorite protagonist. With that being stated, one of the reviews is actually from a resident of Los Santos.

The review reads, “Illuminating, revelatory, heartbreaking, and pulse-quickening - and that’s before you’ve even finished the editor’s forward.” This review came from Alison Taylor from the Los Santos Book Review.

In a recent development, there is an obscure reference to GTA 5 in GTA 6, and it connects back to some of the promotional material for GTA 5. One of the trailers for GTA 5 featured a man with a newspaper on his desk.

It has been revealed that if you are paying attention, you can see that the newspaper’s headline reads, “Aliens ate my prize [blank]. Of course, I have to bleep out the final word due to vulgarity, but it connected to GTA 4, and it also played into the insane satirical nature of GTA 5.

This same newspaper has returned, and it is in GTA 6. In a shack in the Grassrivers, you can spot the same newspaper sitting on a table. It is amazing that Rockstar remembered to bring back this strange newspaper.

Floyd and Debora Hebert were an unhappy couple living in Vespucci Beach in GTA 5. Their house is used as a safehouse by Trevor and their cousin Wade. However, they don’t survive the events of GTA 5, as Trevor murders them in a brutal off-screen killing that leaves him covered in blood.

It is never known exactly what happened after that event, but you can learn the truth of what transpired after the events of GTA 5 by listening to the radio in GTA 6.

If you listen to the crime thriller podcast channel on the radio, you will hear them talk about Floyd and Debora. It turns out that Wade got blamed for their deaths.

Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood.
  • The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.
  • Bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood. A new study from Johns Hopkins University found that people with lower bone density in their spine experienced faster cognitive decline and more rapid deterioration of the brain's white matter as they aged.

The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.

Bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone. Lower density makes bones more fragile and increases the likelihood of fractures. Although the effects of bone loss on skeletal health are well established, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how declining bone density might relate to changes in the brain.

Using AI to Investigate Bone Density and Brain Health.

It has been revealed that to explore this connection, a research team led by Sara Momtazmanesh, M.D., a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Sciences at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, examined existing data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). The analysis included information from participants who had undergone chest CT scans without contrast dye, multiple types of brain MRI examinations, and tests measuring cognitive performance.

Industry observers note that the researchers applied a deep learning algorithm developed in the laboratory of Shadpour Demehri, M.D., a Johns Hopkins professor of radiology. The AI system analyzed non-contrast chest CT images from 2,086 MESA participants to determine their initial thoracic vertebral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), a measurement of bone density in the spine.

Of those participants, 715 had the required bone density measurements along with brain MRI results and cognitive testing, making them eligible for the final study group.

The researchers examined the MRI scans for two indicators of changes in the brain's white matter. The first was white matter hyperintensities, areas of abnormal tissue that appear unusually bright on certain MRI images. The second was reduced fractional anisotropy, a measurement that can indicate deterioration in the microscopic organization of white matter. Both types of changes have been associated with cognitive decline and a greater risk of dementia.

Follow-up imaging data were available for 408 participants for white matter hyperintensities and 405 participants for fractional anisotropy, allowing researchers to examine how these brain changes progressed over time.

Lower Bone Density Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline.

The analysis revealed a notable pattern: participants with lower spinal bone density at the beginning of the study tended to experience a faster decline in overall cognitive performance.

Sources indicate that the researchers also identified changes in specific brain regions that are notable for thinking and memory. Lower bone density was associated with greater accumulation of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum, a structure that supports executive function, working memory, and attention.

According to recent reports, another connection emerged in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, a brain region involved in executive function. Participants with lower bone density demonstrated a more pronounced decline in fractional anisotropy in this area, suggesting worsening white matter integrity.

"This study is the first longitudinal secondary analysis linking baseline vertebral bone mineral density to changes in white matter structure, white matter hyperintensity progression and cognition," Dr. Demehri mentioned. "This comprehensive study using both imaging and clinical assessments sends a clear signal that bone density at baseline is associated with both functional and imaging measures of age-related brain degeneration.".

Despite the connection between weaker bones and declining brain health, the researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish that osteoporosis causes dementia.

Instead, bone deterioration and brain degeneration may be consequences of some of the same biological changes that occur with aging.

Industry observers note that "This study is not about cause and effect, but rather the observation of a metabolic syndrome that may cause both bone and brain degeneration," Dr. Demehri mentioned. "The co-occurrence observed in the study may reflect shared metabolic drivers of aging, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and menopausal change, rather than a direct bone-to-brain effect.".

According to recent reports, these findings raise the possibility that identifying people with reduced bone density could also help recognize those at greater risk of neurological decline. Earlier identification might create opportunities for additional screening and better management of risk factors that affect both skeletal and brain health.

Routine CT Scans Could Reveal Hidden Signs of Brain Aging.

One potentially valuable implication of the research is that doctors may be able to obtain useful information about bone density from CT scans that patients have already received for unrelated medical reasons.

"Chest CT is done for lung cancer screening, calcium scoring, nodule follow-up, and many other indications," Dr. Momtazmanesh mentioned. "These scans could provide an opportunistic measurement of bone density from the thoracic spine that is associated with a loss of cognitive function.".

By using AI to analyze existing medical images, researchers may be able to identify patterns of age-related disease that would otherwise go unnoticed. This approach could also help scientists investigate why conditions affecting different parts of the body often develop together.

It has been revealed that dr. Demehri concurred: "Diagnostic images contain an immense amount of data that AI can now synthesize at scale across multiple organ systems. This creates a robust, newly feasible opportunity to interconnect co-existing age-related pathologies that have traditionally been studied in isolation and to identify shared biological pathways and potential common causal mechanisms.".

It has been revealed that the study highlights a potentially important connection between bone health and cognitive function, while also demonstrating how AI could make routine medical imaging more informative. Although further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms involved, the findings suggest that measurements taken from the spine may provide valuable clues about changes occurring in the aging brain.

The study, "Deep Learning-derived Bone Mineral Density and Longitudinal White Matter Microstructure and Cognitive Decline: Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis," also included Quincy A. Hathaway, M.D., Ph.D., Michael P. Bancks, Ph.D., M.P.H., David A. Bluemke, M.D., M.S.B., Ph.D., R. Graham Barr, M.D., Dr.P.H., Wendy S. Post, M.D., M.S., Mohamad Habes, Ph.D., Ilya Nasrallah, M.D., Ph.D., Susan R. Heckbert, M.D., Ph.D., R. Nick Bryan, M.D., Ph.D., Jose A. Luchsinger, M.D., M.P.H., Mei Wan, Ph.D., Matthew Budoff, M.D., João A. C. Lima, M.D., M.B.A., Timothy M. Hughes, Ph.D., M.P.H., and Christos Davatzikos, Ph.D., who collaborated with Drs. Demehri and Momtazmanesh.

Recent findings suggest that nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically debuted first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

The Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another massive reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

In a recent development, the demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

In a recent development, this time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that marvel Cosmic Invasion was a bit of a dream game for me; I loved the X-Men arcade game in the '90s, so when Tribute Games released the excellent Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge in 2022, I immediately hoped they'd revitalize other licensed brawler franchises released by Konami in the late '80s and early '90s. While we still haven't heard any word of a newly introduced brawler starring The Simpsons, Tribute did follow up its Turtle triumph with Marvel Cosmic Invasion, another throwback side-scrolling beat 'em up, this time starring Marvel's mightiest.

In a recent development, I played through Marvel Cosmic Invasion multiple times and had a blast, but I moved on quickly, as I didn't feel the need to collect different palette-swaps of the many heroes on offer. Even after Cyclops and The Thing joined the roster as DLC in May, I still saw Cosmic Invasion as a game in the rearview. That changes this week, as The Siege of Castle Doom not only adds two additional playable characters (Invisible Woman and Doctor Doom), but also a mode that has the potential to bring me back for more runs for the foreseeable future.

Seeing that Annihilus is threatening the universe, Doom decides to take matters into his own hands. Unfortunately, much in the way that it seems that he may try to fix the multiversal incursions in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, Victor Von Doom's solution in Marvel Cosmic Invasion – the Cosmic Inductor – would lead to untold death and destruction. In The Siege of Castle Doom, you select your team and fight your way through various floors of the stronghold belonging to the man who is perhaps Marvel's greatest villain. Your goal is to fight through the winding, randomized hallways of Castle Doomstadt, charging Reed Richards' Stabilizer and tactically bolstering your team along the way, before Doctor Doom can enact his proposal.

As for the latest playable characters, Doctor Doom is less agile, but his attacks pack a whallop, while Invisible Woman's force fields and speed make her the more versatile pick. I don't know that I see either of them replacing my mains from the base game, but I had fun experimenting with them throughout this mode. Regardless of which character you choose from the expanding roster, you still must traverse Castle Doomstadt before Doom achieves his objective.

Fighting through waves of enemies across differently themed and booby-trapped rooms, you encounter all manner of foes from the base game, as well as upcoming minion types from Doom. When you defeat enemies, they drop batteries that charge your Stabilizer, letting you even the odds and stop Doom. Conversely, each time an enemy hits your character, it charges Doom's Cosmic Inductor, inching him closer to victory and making his minions faster and stronger in the process. As you might expect, the rooms get harder the deeper you go, and while each player starts with two characters to swap between, if a character completely depletes their health, they're gone for good, making it even tougher. As such, you need to keep your eyes on each character's health and swap them out when it makes sense.

Industry observers note that as you complete each room, you can choose which path to take to augment your characters with new special abilities. True to the roguelite structure, as you complete rooms, you can also buff your characters' stats within the run. Certain rooms offer extra batteries to help your Stabilizer charge, while others offer new and upgraded equipment. There's also one that promises random events that can easily alter the trajectory of your run for better or worse. Though I often enjoyed boosting attack stats to make enemies less like damage sponges, I had to balance that against buffing their health to keep them alive and charging the Stabilizer to have a fighting chance.

Beyond the in-run upgrades and modifiers, you can also amp up the action run-over-run through upgrades in Reed's Lab, which add to the pool of modifiers you can select from at the start of each run. The expansion also adds new palettes for existing heroes, plus new music by composer Tee Lopes. While I've only done a few runs of The Siege of Castle Doom (each taking between 45 and 90 minutes, depending on how successful you are), I feel a revitalized sense of excitement for Marvel Cosmic Invasion. Tribute claims completionists can spend upwards of 15 hours in this new mode, which has me champing at the bit to dive back into what will likely be my primary way of interacting with Marvel Cosmic Invasion going forward.

Marvel Cosmic Invasion – The Siege of Castle Doom is available today on all platforms, and it is a strong addition to an already great game. You can read our review of the base version of Marvel Cosmic Invasion here.

Sources indicate that earlier this very month, Jensen Huang, CEO of the world’s leading chip producer, Nvidia, not to mention one of the most crucial companies to the advancement of gaming as a creator of GPUs, was wracked with controversy. Huang admitted an affair with a woman alleged to be a spy for the Chinese government and was also accused of an affair with an Nvidia executive, according to the BBC.

Sources indicate that following all of these revelations, Huang voluntarily resigned from his position as CEO. For a brief, glorious moment, the gaming community breathed a sigh of relief, as it was Huang’s gung-ho attitude on AI-centric developments over all else that had largely contributed to Nvidia shifting focus away from gaming hardware. Maybe we’d start seeing affordable, optimized GPUs again!

It has been revealed that unfortunately, we are not allowed to have nice things in this timeline. According to a BBC report this morning, following a unanimous vote from the current Nvidia corporate board, Huang has been officially reinstated to his position as CEO. Yay.

According to the BBC report, despite previous insistences from the board that Huang would not be reinstated to his position, the ultimate conclusion that they came to is that only Huang could continue the AI-focused push Nvidia has been running with lately.

"The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," the board’s current chair remarked in a public statement on the Nvidia website.

The ultimate conclusion that they came to is that only Huang could continue the AI-focused push Nvidia has been running with lately.

Apparently, Huang’s return was orchestrated at least in part by United States President Donald Trump, who, in a brief interview with CNBC, said that he “felt very strongly that [Huang] should come back, and we've done a very thorough investigation.

"And the investigation showed that he did - I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents - but he did nothing wrong other than he created a chip that's invaluable.".

Following news of Huang’s reinstatement, Nvidia’s stock value bounced up 32%, a notable increase following a 13% drop-off at the end of last week.

In a personal statement on the Nvidia website, Huang said that he is “honoured to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a upcoming industrial revolution.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

Some analysts speculate that, particularly within the AI-centric tech field, figureheads have become an important part of the push. Parallels have been drawn between Huang’s reinstatement and that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was reinstated in his own position just five days after being fired from it in 2023.

The BBC’s tech and AI analyst Zoe Kleinman posited on the matter, saying that “It indicates a lot that despite the serious accusations made about him and his affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy, ultimately his position in the tech industry has proved to be more important:.

“There had been many calls for him to be reinstated - including from within the UK House of Lords - on the grounds that the AI industry would be weaker without him.”.

Whatever the precise reason, it’s probably a safe bet that Nvidia will promptly resume its previous course, which means those of us in the gaming sphere won’t be seeing any affordable GPUs any time soon. Oh well, it was nice to dream of a world where you didn't need to justify buying a top-shelf graphics card...
